summary: A revised Telnet protocol proposal from the committee, circulated for comments. Unless comments arrived within two weeks, they would not be considered for the official Telnet document. It lists the earlier notes it builds on. It was replaced by RFC 495.

eli5.summary: This is the second draft of the long invisible cable plan for logging in to far computers. People had two weeks to say what to change.

subtitle: A May 1971 committee draft of the Telnet protocol, built around a shared 7-bit ASCII Network Virtual Terminal.

tldr.problem: Terminals and processes at one site needed to act like terminals directly connected to a different kind of computer at another site, without each host learning every other host's quirks.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet defines a Network Virtual Terminal that uses 7-bit ASCII sent in 8-bit bytes, with a few control signals marked by a high-order bit of one.
tldr.outcome: This was a proposal circulated for comment, and it was replaced by RFC 495.

facts.label: NVT code
facts.value: 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit bytes, high bit zero

today: This draft updates RFC 139, was updated by RFC 318, and was replaced by RFC 495. It is a historical proposal, not the final Telnet specification.

sections.title: A Proposal Open for Comment
sections.content:
The Telnet committee circulated this RFC to ask for comments, evaluation and requests for modification. Comments that did not reach the writer within two weeks of 19 May 1971 would not be considered for the official Telnet protocol document. The committee felt the protocol was adequate for initial implementation.

Telnet is a third-level protocol. Its function is to make a terminal or process at a using site appear to the system or process at a serving site as logically equivalent to a terminal directly connected there, while minimizing what each host must know about the others.
sections.eli5: A group wrote down a plan and gave everybody two weeks to say what was wrong with it. The plan lets you sit at one computer and use another as if you were right there.

sections.title: Protocol Levels and Sites
sections.content:
The RFC names three levels. Level 1 is the host-IMP protocol (BBN Report 1822). Level 2 is the host-host protocol performed by the Network Control Programs (NCPs). Level 3 is the place the NCP talks to internally in its own host; the Telnet process runs there at a using site, and the Telnet server runs there at a serving site.

The using site is the host where the Telnet process runs. The serving site is the host that receives the user's keyboard input. Telnet relies on the NCP and an Initial Connection Protocol, and it uses a byte size of 8 bits on the permanent connection.
sections.eli5: Think of layers like a postal chain: one layer carries the wires, one carries the messages, and Telnet sits on top where people actually type.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal and Control Codes
sections.content:
Telnet provides a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT). Its code is full 7-bit ASCII, transmitted in eight-bit bytes with the high-order bit set to zero. A line ends with carriage return (X'0D') followed by line feed (X'0A'). The serving site is initially assumed to provide no echo.

The using site must let its users produce all 128 ASCII codes plus a set of Telnet control signals. The ASCII ESC character marks that the next characters have special meaning, defined by the serving site. Control signals that must cross the connection are eight-bit codes with the high-order bit set to one, listed in the table below.

An endnote adds that a one-byte DATA TYPE signal is sent as the first byte over a connection. Other assigned types are X'A1' Transparency, X'A2' EBCDIC, X'A3' and X'A4' for special strings.
sections.eli5: The pretend terminal speaks one simple alphabet. Special secret codes with an extra bit switched on mean things like 'stop' or 'please do not repeat my letters back'.

sections.title: Minimum Implementation
sections.content:
A minimal using site must let a user send all 128 ASCII codes in the 8-bit field, ignore and strip Telnet control characters from the serving site, provide local echo or print, use the CR-LF end-of-line convention, and implement the local controls to transmit all data so far or suppress the end of line.

A minimal serving site must provide and announce a one-for-one mapping between ASCII and its own character and control set (or a subset if its set is larger than 128), ignore and strip control characters from the using site, assume the using site provides local echo, and use CR-LF. The document says it will be revised to cover data types beyond NVT ASCII.
sections.eli5: Each side gets a short checklist of the least it must do to join in: send letters properly, ignore codes it does not understand, and end lines the agreed way.

items.label: DATA TYPE
items.desc: Both sites. Code will be transmitted by NVT, using seven-bit ASCII conventions.

items.label: Send INS
items.desc: Using site. Order the using site NCP to send an INS and insert X'80' in the data stream.

items.label: Break / Attention
items.desc: Using site. Break or Attention, and reverse break.

items.label: Hide your input
items.desc: Serving site. Suppress printing of a password.
